agricultural-science-2021-HL-paper-p39-i.alt: The Question 16(d) virtual fencing item. Centred "Or", then "(d) The application of technology in Agriculture is increasing. agricultural-science-2021-HL-paper-p45-i.alt: The Question 18(c) lactation graph, complete. The line "(c) Analyse the graph showing the lactation period of a dairy cow and answer the questions which follow." sits above a schematic curve diagram that has NO numbered axes and no units — time runs left to right, energy runs bottom to top. Two curves run across the chart: a dark green curve labelled "Energy requirement" (label in green just after the peak) and a second curve that is dark maroon-red where it lies below the green curve and blue where it lies above it, labelled "Energy intake" (blue label in a box at the left). Both dip slightly, then rise steeply to a peak and fall away to the right. Between the two curves in the rising/peak phase is a bright yellow filled area carrying a diagonal orange banner with the words "Negative Energy Balance"; after the two curves cross (marked by a maroon dashed vertical line) the intake curve lies above the requirement curve and the gap is filled pale blue-green with a diagonal banner reading "Excess energy". A black square-dotted vertical line near the left of centre is captioned "Calving" at the top; a yellow square-dotted vertical line at the right is captioned "Drying off" at the top; two further yellow dotted verticals bracket an orange horizontal bar low in the plot labelled "Transition phase", which straddles calving. A thick red double-headed horizontal arrow labelled "Challenging period" runs from calving to the maroon dashed crossing line. Pale yellow vertical bands shade the far left of the chart and the region to the right of drying off. Along the bottom is a blue banner divided into four labelled stages, left to right: "Dry phase", "Early lactation", "Mid lactation", "Late lactation", with a lighter blue unlabelled segment at the far right. Attribution "(Adapted from Shauman, 2015)". Below the graph, "(i) Explain what is the drying off period." with its answer box and "(ii) Outline one reason for the negative energy balance in early lactation." with the top of its box.

the second curve (maroon where below the green curve, blue where above it), printed label in a box at the left of the chart

the pale blue-green filled area after the curves cross, where intake exceeds requirement, named on a diagonal banner
the black square-dotted vertical line near the left of centre
the yellow square-dotted vertical line towards the right
the red double-headed horizontal arrow spanning from calving to the point where the two curves cross
the orange horizontal bar low in the plot, straddling calving between two yellow dotted verticals
first segment of the blue stage banner along the bottom, before calving
second segment of the blue stage banner, immediately after calving

agricultural-science-2021-OL-paper-p19-i.alt: Question 13 part (a) stimulus. Below the heading Question 13 and the instruction Read the following article on liver fluke and answer the questions which follow is a boxed newspaper-style article whose text reads: Liver fluke thrive in the Irish wet climate. It is estimated to cost Irish farmers over 90 million euro annually. It is an issue in both cattle and sheep, but sheep are often the most badly affected. It affects all ages of sheep as it is picked up off the grass when sheep are grazing. This commonly occurs in the autumn and winter months. A shows a uniform stand of narrow green grass blades, all of one type and much the same height, growing from a dark brown topsoil layer; their roots are short, fine, reddish-brown and fibrous and stay entirely within the top band of soil. Both blocks share the same layered profile: dark brown topsoil, a darker brown band, a tan stony subsoil with scattered grey stones and a grey stony layer at the base. agricultural-science-2025-OL-paper-p12-i.alt: Full crop of Question 10 — text on the left, diagram on the right. The stem reads 'The diagram shows the process of sex sorting bull semen.' The diagram is a vertical flow schematic of a sperm-sorting machine, read top to bottom. At the top, two sperm cells travel down a narrow channel drawn as two dark blue vertical bars; the upper sperm head carries a pink X, the lower one a blue Y, and a red arrow labelled with a bold red A points to that lower sperm cell with the blue Y in its head. Below the channel a single sperm with a pink X passes through a dark blue ellipse (the detector ring). Next, a sperm with a blue Y passes between two short black bars marked with a teal plus sign on the left and a teal minus sign on the right (the charging plates). Below that the stream splits into two: a sperm with a blue Y tagged with a teal minus symbol on the left, and a sperm with a pink X tagged with a teal plus symbol on the right. At the bottom the sorted cells fall into three cylinders — a blue cylinder labelled Y at the left receiving the minus-charged Y sperm, a pink cylinder labelled X at the right receiving the plus-charged X sperm, and a dark green cylinder in the centre receiving two sperm whose heads carry a green question mark, with a red arrow and the words 'Dead and abnormal sperm' pointing to it. On the left of the crop are part (a) with a blank answer box, part (b) with a small blue-shaded tick table whose rows are labelled X and Y, and part (c) with a blank numbered answer table.

maths-2023-HL-ask-p2-q8-b-i.alt: The question as printed on the paper — An online word game involves trying to guess a five-letter word in as few attempts as possible. For this game, each player is given a score s, where s∈ℝ, based on how many attempts it takes them to guess the word. In Ireland, players’ scores are approximately normally distributed, with a mean of 3·87 and a standard deviation of 0·36. A player is selected at random from the players in Ireland. Find the probability that this player has a score of less than 3·5. A random sample of 64 Galway players has a mean score of 3·74. Based on this, a local newspaper claims that Galway players have a different mean score to players in Ireland.

maths-2023-HL-ask-p2-q8-d-ii.alt: The question as printed on the paper — An online word game involves trying to guess a five-letter word in as few attempts as possible. maths-2013-HL-ask-p1-project-q7-a.alt: The question as printed on the paper — A stadium can hold 25 000 people. People attending a regular event at the stadium must purchase a ticket in advance. The results of a survey carried out by the owners suggest that for every €1 reduction, from €20, in the ticket price, the expected attendance would increase by 1000 people. maths-2013-HL-ask-p1-q3-a.alt: The question as printed on the paper — Scientists can estimate the age of certain ancient items by measuring the proportion of carbon–14, relative to the total carbon content in the item. The formula used is Q = e^(−0·693t/5730), where Q is the proportion of carbon–14 remaining and t is the age, in years, of the item. An item is 2000 years old. Use the formula to find the proportion of carbon–14 in the item.
maths-2013-HL-ask-p1-q3-a.attribution: SEC Leaving Certificate Mathematics 2013 Higher Level — © State Examinations Commission

maths-2013-HL-ask-p1-q3-b.alt: The question as printed on the paper — Scientists can estimate the age of certain ancient items by measuring the proportion of carbon–14, relative to the total carbon content in the item. maths-2013-HL-ask-p1-q4-a-i.alt: The question as printed on the paper — Niamh has saved to buy a car. maths-2013-HL-ask-p1-q4-a-ii.alt: The question as printed on the paper — Niamh has saved to buy a car. maths-2013-HL-ask-p1-q4-b.alt: The question as printed on the paper — Conall borrowed to buy a car. He borrowed €15 000 at a monthly interest rate of 0·866%. He made 36 equal monthly payments to repay the entire loan. How much, to the nearest euro, was each of his monthly payments?

maths-2013-HL-ask-p1-q5-a.alt: The question as printed on the paper — A stadium can hold 25 000 people. People attending a regular event at the stadium must purchase a ticket in advance. When the ticket price is €20, the expected attendance at an event is 12 000 people. The results of a survey carried out by the owners suggest that for every €1 reduction, from €20, in the ticket price, the expected attendance would increase by 1000 people. If the ticket price was €18, how many people would be expected to attend?
maths-2013-HL-ask-p1-q5-a.attribution: SEC Leaving Certificate Mathematics 2013 Higher Level — © State Examinations Commission

maths-2013-HL-ask-p1-q5-b.alt: The question as printed on the paper — A stadium can hold 25 000 people. People attending a regular event at the stadium must purchase a ticket in advance. The results of a survey carried out by the owners suggest that for every €1 reduction, from €20, in the ticket price, the expected attendance would increase by 1000 people. Let x be the ticket price, where x ≤ 20. Write down, in terms of x, the expected attendance at such an event.
maths-2013-HL-ask-p1-q5-b.attribution: SEC Leaving Certificate Mathematics 2013 Higher Level — © State Examinations Commission

Suppose that tickets are instead priced at a value that is expected to give a full attendance at the stadium. Find the difference between the income from the sale of tickets at this price and the maximum income calculated at (e) above.

maths-2013-HL-ask-p1-q5-g.alt: The question as printed on the paper — The stadium can hold 25 000 people. The stadium was full for a recent special event. If 1000 more family tickets had been sold, the income from the event would have been reduced by €14 000. How many family tickets were sold?
maths-2013-HL-ask-p1-q5-g.attribution: SEC Leaving Certificate Mathematics 2013 Higher Level — © State Examinations Commission

maths-2013-FL-ask-p1-q4-b.alt: The question as printed on the paper — Mary buys a new car costing €26 000. The garage gives her €8400 for her old car and she has savings of €5600. How much interest will she pay?

maths-2011-HL-ask-p1-project-q4-c.alt: The question as printed on the paper — In a science experiment, Q(t) was observed at t = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 seconds, giving 2.920, 2.642, 2.391, 2.163, 1.957 respectively. Q(t) = Ae^(−bt), where A and b are constants. Show that Q(t) is a constant multiple of Q(t − 1) for t ≥ 1. Find k such that Q(t + k) = ½Q(t) for all t ≥ 0, correct to two decimal places.

maths-2011-HL-ask-p1-project-q5-a.alt: The question as printed on the paper — Gold jewellery has carat rating c = 24m_g/m_t, where m_g is its gold mass and m_t its total mass. The jeweller has 147 g of 9-carat gold and 85 g of 18-carat gold. Its value is its gold content only, at €36 per gram. What is the total value of the jeweller’s stock of old jewellery?
